Question: Why did Russian monarchists apparently disappear overnight after the Revolutions of 1917? Why did the entire population go from worshipping the Tsar to not thinking about him at all in a finger snap?
Answer: False premise. Anti-monarchist sentiments had been building in Russia for decades. Members of the Russian nihilist movement carried out a number of assassination attempts against the tsars since the 1860s, culminating in the assassination of Tsar Alexander II by bomb in 1881. Tsar Nicholas II, the last tsar of Russia, was never popular, and that sentiment only increased among the Russian people throughout his 23 year reign. In particular he was criticized and hated for repressing his political opponents and ignoring numerous internal injustices such as the anti-Jewish pogroms, his belief that he was ordained by God to rule Russia and could thus ignore the limits of his power put in place by the Russian constitution, and his decision to involve Russia in a series of costly wars. He was also mocked and disrespected due to his family's obsession with the mystic Rasputin. During his reign Russia experienced unprecedented unrest. The first anti-tsarist revolution took place from 1905 to 1907 and included labor strikes, military mutiny, and the demand for a more democratic government. Nicholas II eventually conceded and allowed the creation of the State Duma, an elected legislative council similar to the House of Commons in British Parliament. However, Nicholas II limited the State Duma's authority, continued to hold ultimate authority in political matters, and granted himself the ability to dissolve the State Duma whenever he wanted, which he did three times in a decade. The final straw was in 1914 when Nicholas II, against the advice of his counselors, declared war on Austria-Hungary and subsequently their ally Germany, triggering WWI. Russia was ill-prepared for war, lacking modern military equipment and infrastructure, and Russia lacked the industrialization necessary to modernize its armies. As a consequence Russia suffered a series of disastrous defeats resulting in the deaths of 1.5–2 million Russian soldiers. Confidence in the monarchy collapsed completely, triggering riots, military mutinies, the resignation of most of the Russian government, and shortly the October Revolution which led to the formation of the Soviet Union. Faced with a brewing revolution, Nicholas II abdicated the throne in March of 1917 and he was placed under house arrest shortly after. He and his family were eventually assassinated by Soviet revolutionaries a year later in 1918. So, no, the entire population didn't worship the tsar. Revolutions don't happen overnight, they are the result of years and often decades of unrest resulting from unaddressed grievances and injustice. Revolutionary thinking had been building in Russia for at least half a century before the Russian monarchy was ended. Question: What is the tastiest animal that is now extinct?
Answer: I'm going to go with the Steller's sea cow. The Steller's sea cow was a large relative of manatees and dugongs that once lived along the coastlines of the northern Pacific Ocean. These gentle giants grazed on kelp and grew to a massive 9 meters (30 ft) long and weighed up to 10 tons. They were first scientifically described in 1741 by German naturalist Georg Wilhelm Steller, after whom the animal was named. Steller described the sea cow's meat as delicious, comparing it to corned beef though with a tougher texture. The thick fat and blubber tasted like almonds and was used as a cooking oil or sometimes just drunk as a hot beverage. The sea cow’s milk was thick and rich and was used as a beverage or to make butter. European explorers weren't the only ones hunting the sea cow, either. Both the indigenous Aleut people of Alaska's Aleutian Islands and the indigenous Siberian Yupik people had been hunting them for thousands of years. This hunting, combined with climate change caused by the end of the last Ice Age, had caused the Steller's sea cow populations to dwindle, and by the time the first Europeans saw the animals they were reduced to an estimated population of 2,000 individuals living around two small islands off the east coast of the Kamchatka penninsula. Fur trappers, seal hunters, and whalers soon began making stops at the islands to hunt the slow, buoyant sea cows as an easy food source, and by 1768 - a mere 27 years after their scientific description - the Steller's sea cow was extinct.

Question: Was The Elephant Man a poorly directed movie? No plot twists and a ridiculously predictable script. It had to be David Lynch's worst movie, like he threw it together with no thought.
Answer: David Lynch did not write most of the script. Producer Jonathan Sanger purchased the script from screenwriters Christopher De Vore and Eric Bergren, and the screenplay was mostly complete when Lynch was selected to direct. Lynch's main contributions to the script were the surrealist elements bookending the film. Anyway, to answer your question, no, the film is not poorly directed. The Elephant Man was nominated for eight Oscars, including Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Adapted Screenplay. That last nomination is important. You see, the script for The Elephant Man is based on the true story of Joseph Merrick, a Victorian-era Englishman with a degenerative physical disorder that gave him increasingly severe physical deformities. Question: Does Jupiter eclipse the outer planets?
Answer: Yes, but nowhere near as dramatically as the Moon eclipsing the Sun here on Earth. Here on Earth solar eclipses are so dramatic because the Moon's umbra - the part of its shadow formed where the Sun is completely obscured - can reach a narrow band of Earth's surface. In this area (known as totality), the entire surface of the Sun is blocked from view by the Moon, allowing those in the area to see the Sun's outermost layer, the corona, as well as any large solar flares that may be present at the time. However, eclipses this dramatic only happen on Earth because - due to their diameters and distances - the relative size of the Sun and Moon are coincidentally very similar as viewed from Earth. However, none of the planets are large enough or close enough to each other to create a similar effect. Instead what we see are a type of eclipse known as a solar transit. This is when a body passes between the Sun and another body, partially obscuring the Sun. The most commonly seen solar transits on Earth occur when Mercury and/or Venus pass between the Sun and Earth. A solar transit of Venus These transits result in a measurable drop in the Sun's luminosity, though it is usually not enough to be noticeable with the naked eye. However, such transits can sometimes be seen during sunset. Any planet can create a solar transit for any of the more distant planets in the solar system, and in fact we can observe such stellar transits in other solar systems - this is one of the main ways we discover exoplanets in fact. Jupiter is no different. Question: Were pigs originally created using human DNA?
Answer: Modern pigs are the domesticated form of the Eurasian wild boar. The wild boar first evolved around one million years ago in Southeast Asia and gradually spread across much of the rest of Asia, much of Europe, and northern Africa. The first anatomically modern humans (Homo sapiens) evolved in Central Africa around 300,000 years ago, meaning the wild boar is more than three times older than modern humans. Humans first domesticated pigs around 11,000 years ago in the Middle East and again independently in East Asia around 8,000 years ago. DNA wasn't discovered until 1869 by Swiss biochemist Friedrich Miescher and the first gene-splice (ie, the introduction of one species’ DNA into the genetic code of another) didn't occur until 1971. Pigs and humans last shared a common ancestor around 105 million years ago in the late Cretaceous. It would have looked something like this: So, no. Pigs were not originally created with human DNA.

Question: What was it like during the Roman Empire if you had contamination OCD? I mean, just imagine community bathing and the sponges on a stick instead of toilet paper?
Answer: Contamination OCD almost certainly didn't exist back then (although other forms of OCD most likely did). Contamination OCD is based on an overwhelming fear or preoccupation with the spread of germs. The Germ Theory of disease didn't exist in Roman times. Romans believed disease was caused by an imbalance of the humours. According to this theory humans have four bodily fluids, or “humours,” namely phlegm, blood, yellow bile, and black bile. Disease was presumed to be caused by an excess or deficit of one or more of the humours. The humoral system was common throughout the Mediterranean region and later throughout Europe. It likely originated in Egypt and was later adopted by the ancient Greeks and Romans. The humoral system remained the prevailing disease theory in western medicine until its popularity began to decline in the late 1700s, though it wasn't until the 1850s that it was replaced entirely with the germ theory. That said, while it's extremely unlikely any Romans were worrying about contamination from germs, it's entirely possible that some of them were excessively focused on cleanliness. Romans were quite fastidious in their personal hygiene and regularly bathed themselves, often washing their face, hands, and feet even more frequently. It's possible that someone who was very concerned about cleanliness would have bathed more often and more privately (people went to the public baths more for the social aspect than strictly out of necessity). As for the toilets, the first thing you have to know about the xylospongium (what the Romans called the sponge on a stick) is that historians actually disagree on whether they were used to clean the backside after defecation or whether they were the ancient Roman equivalent of a modern toilet brush. The discovery of fragments of cloth in an ancient Roman septic tank in the city of Herculaneum indicates that the Romans may have used disposable cloth scraps to wipe themselves rather than a communal sponge. Regardless of how they were used, the xylospongium wasn't simply left sitting in the open covered in feces. After use it was rinsed in running water and then soaked in a jar of vinegar or brine. This was done to eliminate odors but it had the unknown (yet fortunate) side effect of sterilizing the sponge as well.

Question: What is the conservation status of Coelacanth? Does this fish make good pets for home aquariums?
Answer: There are two species of coelacanth: the Indonesian Coelacanth (Latimeria menadoensis) and the West Indian Ocean Coelacanth (Latimeria chalumnae). The West Indian Ocean species is critically endangered and estimates put the species’ population at around 500 or fewer. The Indonesian species is doing better, but is still listed as “vulnerable” as it is estimated that there are fewer than 10,000 individuals alive. Neither one can be kept in a home aquarium. Coelacanths can grow larger than most people. They often reach lengths greater than 2 meters (more than 6.5 feet) and weigh up to 90 kg (200 lbs). They can also live longer than most people: the oldest ever caught was 84 years old and it is estimated that they can live to be more than 100. To make matters worse, coelacanths are deepwater ocean dwellers and typically live in water 200-700 meters (650-2300 ft) deep. They occasionally venture up to shallower water to look for food at night but they return to the depths before daybreak. Saltwater tanks are already notoriously difficult to maintain, so on top of all the work necessary to keep the salt water tank functioning you would also need a way to constantly pressurize the water to 290-1020 psi to keep the coelacanth alive. For comparison, a 1 meter deep unpressurized aquarium will exert a pressure of 1.46 psi at the bottom. A 10 meter deep unpressurized aquarium would exert 14.5 psi at the bottom. A school of coelacanths resting in a cave On top of all of that, coelacanth are nocturnal and avoid what little sunlight reaches their depths by sleeping in caves during the day. Not only would you have to contend with everything listed in the paragraph above, you would also need to keep the coelacanth in near darkness in order to not cause it severe distress. No professional aquarium has been able to keep a coelacanth alive longer than one day. There's no way one could survive in a home aquarium.

Question: How big was the risk of lightning strike to a medieval knight that was wearing metal armor and weapon during a rainy battlefield?
Answer: It depends. Contrary to popular belief metal does not attract lightning. Lightning will strike the tallest object in the area regardless of its material, sometimes to disastrous consequences: In 2023 the historical First Congregational Church in Spencer Massachusetts was struck by lightning on its steeple and burned down. The building was all-wood construction and dated back to 1863. Fortunately no one was hurt. The myth that lightning is attracted to metal may have arisen after the invention of lightning rods in the 1700s. They don't attract lightning, rather the metal conducts the electricity away from the other more electrically-resistant building materials. So with that said, the knight was only really in danger if he was the tallest object on the battlefield. Since most medieval battles took place in open fields and knights were cavalry soldiers this was a possibility, especially if he was carrying his lance upright like so: However, there were others at risk as well. Standard bearers would carry their lord's heraldic banner into battle so his soldiers had a point of reference in the chaos of battle: But those most in danger of lightning strikes would have been the pikemen. Pikes were the primary weapon of medieval European warfare and were typically wielded by peasants and mercenaries who would have been too poor to afford full plate armor, if they could afford any metal armor at all. While a knight's lance was typically 6–10 ft long (and tended to be on the shorter end since they were wielded one-handed), pikes could be anywhere between 10-23 ft and were usually carried upright until just before combat to reduce strain on the wielder's muscles. Positioning would also play a factor: since lightning always strikes the tallest object in the area, those on the top of a hill would be at greater risk than those in the bottom of a valley. So to sum up, the answer to the question is dependent on a lot of variables, including the knight's location, how they are holding their weapon, and the presence and nature of the polearms on the battlefield.

Question: Despite no fossil evidence, is it possible that polar bears once inhabited The American Great Lakes region in the last Ice Age?
Answer: Probably not. Polar bears are adapted to an aquatic lifestyle and spend most of their time in or very near the ocean, so much so that they are classified as an aquatic mammal. Question: In Star Trek, when the captain says, “red alert” or “battle stations” it’s usually followed by, “shields up”, “load photon torpedoes”, etc. Shouldn’t “red alert” be a blanket order? One that includes all necessary orders for each department?
Answer: Not at all. Red Alert is called when the ship is in danger. However, not all dangers are the same. Let's say it's the Dominion War and the USS Example encounters a Jem'Hadar attack ship. Raising shields is a prudent decision in this situation but arming weapons could be viewed by the approaching ship as a threat and trigger an unnecessary escalation into open combat. Raising the shields and arming weapons would simply accelerate the power drain and reduce the amount of time the crew has to purge the virus from the computer network. There is an endless smorgasbord of space disasters a Federation starship could encounter in its exploration of the galaxy. There is no one-size-fits-all response to them, which is why it is the responsibility of the captain and senior staff to determine the best course of action whenever they encounter such a disaster. Edit: A number of commenters are stating that Red Alert means that weapons and shields are automatically brought online. In response I'll quote the TNG Technical Manual, page 168 (emphasis mine): Red Alert situations, by their very nature, frequently involve unforeseeable variables and unpredictable circumstances. Question: Why did historic people abandon bronze in making tools and weapons and adopt iron instead?
Answer: Iron ore is much more common than copper and tin ores, the components of bronze. Refined iron is also harder and more durable than bronze, meaning that iron tools and weapons will last longer, break less frequently, and hold their shape and sharpness longer than bronze ones. The main reason bronze was used predominantly in antiquity was because the components of bronze have a much lower melting point than iron. Iron's melting point at sea level is 1,538°C (2,800°F), whereas the melting points of copper and tin are 1,085°C (1,984°F) and 232°C (450°F) respectively. Early metallurgists didn't have the technology to get their smelters hot enough to refine iron ore but could get them hot enough to smelt bronze. Once the technology advanced enough to allow iron smelting most metallurgists switched to the stronger and more abundant metal.

Question: How likely is it that someone is actually doing the same research and experiments that were done in the jurassic Park movie?
Answer: Sorry to disappoint, but the likelihood is absolutely none. The chemical structure of DNA can only last a certain amount of time before it breaks down and dissolves. The half-life of DNA is only 521 years. This means that for a sample of DNA, an average of 50% of it decomposes every 521 years. After another 521 years about 50% of the remaining DNA is destroyed, and so on. Under absolutely ideal conditions the longest any part of a DNA molecule can last is around 2 million years, and under normal circumstances it is completely destroyed in a few dozen millenia. Non-avian dinosaurs went extinct during or shortly after the Chicxulub Impact event 66 million years ago. Even if we could find a mosquito trapped in amber that had fed on a dinosaur, there would be no dinosaur DNA to extract from its stomach. Heck, we have an actual dinosaur tail that was preserved in amber, complete with feathers and fossilized skin tissue, but there is no DNA to extract. In both the book and the movie scientists filled in missing DNA sequences with those taken from frogs. If scientists tried to do that in real life, they would end up with: Now, I like frogs as much as the next guy, but I think we can all agree that they aren't dinos. Question: Did Spinosaurus have a round-shaped or square-shaped sail?
Answer: NOTE: This answer has been modified due to me being lazy and not doing proper research the first time. I'm leaving the original answer below since it relates to some discussion in the comments and I want to keep that context. New Answer: No one knows what shape the sail was. Paleontologists have not yet found a complete set of dorsal spines that is fully intact. All specimens found so far have had the tops broken off, and we are uncertain how much is missing. Sailfish use their sails in two ways: first they use the sail to corral fish into a tight ball, then they use the sail to stabilize their bodies as they rapidly slash their long “sword” bill back and forth, striking the fish and injuring or killing them so the sailfish can then eat them. Question: The skeleton of a rabbit looks like the skeleton of some hideous creature rather than a cute bunny, so is it likely that our depictions of dinosaurs, based off their skeletons, could be completely wrong?
Answer: There was actually a problem in paleoart for many years called “shrink wrapping.” For a long time, especially in the 90s and 2000s, paleoartists would often draw dinosaurs as essentially skeletons with a thin layer of skin tightly stretched over them like shrink wrap. These depictions tended to show off every hole and divot in the dinosaur’s skull even though in life those areas would be filled with muscle, fat, sinuses, etc. Dinosaurs tended to look like they were one minute away from dying of starvation. Shrink wrapped T-rex A more realistic T-rex Paleontologists would occasionally remark on these inaccurate depictions but it wasn't until a few mischievous but scientifically-minded artists began satirizing the shrink wrapping trend by making depictions of living animals using the same inaccurate style. The results really drove home how unrealistic paleoart had become. Leading the charge were paleoartists John Conway and C. M. Kosemen and paleontologist Darren Naish with their book “All Yesterdays,” first published in 2012. The first half of the book is a history of paleoart and how depictions of prehistoric life have changed over the years, as well as critiques of inaccurate tropes that were commonplace in much of modern paleoart. The second half of the book is a tongue-in-cheek depiction of familiar modern animals reimagined as shrink-wrapped horrors beyond comprehension. Since then paleoartists have moved away from the shrink wrapping trend and actually started putting some meat on those old bones. This is a house cat. How… adorable? A baboon. Naturally, big teeth means constant slavering drool, right? Can you guess what these are? Clockwise from the top: a horse, a rhinoceros, and an elephant. The issue with paleoart is we have very little information to go on. The good news is paleontologists are constantly making new discoveries that further refine our understanding of the millions of species that have gone extinct. Science is an ever-progressing endeavor focused on weeding out inaccurate hypotheses and gradually improving the accuracy of our data. As time progresses we will continue to gain a more accurate understanding of our universe, both past and present, and our depictions of dinosaurs will follow suit.

Question: Did you know that Neptune is blue since it has more water than Earth?
Answer: While it is true that Neptune has more water than Earth, that is not why it is blue. Neptune's water is almost entirely located in its mantle in a hot, extremely dense mix of water, ammonia, and methane ices formed from the crushing force of Neptune's thick atmosphere (it is estimated that the atmospheric pressure at the boundary of Neptune’s mantle is around 10 giga-Pascals or about 100 times the pressure at the bottom of the Marianas Trench). Neptune's atmosphere is estimated to be between 2400–4800 km thick, far too thick for the mantle to be visible from space. Instead the blue coloration comes from the 1.5% of methane gas in Neptune's atmosphere. Methane gas absorbs the red wavelengths of light and reflects the green and blue wavelengths. This reflected light is what gives Neptune its naturally cyan color (the darker blue you may be familiar with was due to an artificial increase in color contrast applied to Voyager 2’s photos to make Neptune’s white cloud layers more visible).

In fact, hitting the nerve with enough force will leave the arm paralyzed for a few seconds. Vulcans are stated to be three times stronger than humans on average, so theoretically they would be able to exert a great deal more pressure on the suprascapular nerve than a human, enough to trigger shock and cause the person to pass out. Question: How would paleontologists be able to tell if crocodiles had scutes if they had no living ones to reference?
Answer: Crocodyliform “scutes” are more accurately described as “osteoderms.” These have a bony base to which the keratin that forms the outer layer is attached. The bony parts of the osteoderms will fossilize just as readily as the rest of the skeleton, and fossil crocodyliform osteoderms are a fairly common fossil find (you can typically buy them online for around $20–40). Platysuchus, a Jurassic Era crocodyliform showing the osteoderms on its back quite clearly Simosuchus, a small Cretaceous Era herbivorous crocodyliform with very pronounced osteoderm armor Crocodyliforms aren't the only animals with osteoderms. They evolved independently in several other lineages including lizards, armadillos, the African spiny mouse, and a South American species of frog called Gastrotheca weinlandii. Gecko with osteoderms on its head Armadillo skeleton with osteoderm armor Gastrotheca weinlandii skeleton with osteoderms covering its back Osteoderms are also found in numerous extinct groups such as multiple lineages of non-avian dinosaurs (most famously the ankylosaurs and stegosaurs), temnospondyls (an extinct lineage of amphibians), hupehsuchians (a type of ichthyosaur), and my personal favorite prehistoric round boys, the glyptodonts. An exceptionally well preserved fossil of a nodosaurus (a type of ankylosaur) showing its osteoderms Fossilized armor plates from the shoulder of the temnospondyl species Plagiosuchus pustuliferus, with osteoderms visible as small bumps. Glyptodont fossil showing its protective osteoderm armor So even if the crocodyliform lineage was completely extinct paleontologists would find fossilized osteoderms in close association with crocodyliform skeletons (if not directly attached). They would then be able to easily identify them as osteoderms by comparing their structure and arrangement to other species with osteoderms, both living and extinct.

Question: What is the best season on Venus?
Answer: Venus doesn't have seasons. Seasons are caused by a planet’s axial tilt. As a planet orbits its star one pole is pointed toward the star during one half of its orbit and pointed away during the other. Earth has an axial tilt of 23.5 degrees, which means its poles are tilted 23.5 degrees way from perpendicular to its orbital plane. This is what causes the seasons on Earth. Venus's axial tilt, however, is only 2.6 degrees from perpendicular, far too small of a difference to generate seasonal variations. On top of that, Venus's atmosphere is crushingly thick (93 times denser than Earth's at sea level) and composed almost entirely of carbon dioxide, an insulating greenhouse gas (96.5%). This means that the surface temperature is almost completely uniform across the entire planet all the time, around 464°C (867°F).

Question: Can there be a solar eclipse on other planets? Do their moons have a solid shadow that reaches the surface of their planet?
Answer: As far as the inner planets go, no. Mars is the only rocky planet besides Earth to have moons, and they are far too small. The larger and closer of the two, Phobos, has an average diameter of only 22 km (14 miles), far too small to cast a shadow that would reach Mars's surface. As for the gas giants, eclipses there can be much more common. The Sun appears smaller from the outer planets and some of the moons orbiting the gas planets are larger than Mercury. Jupiter's Galilean moons are so large and close to Jupiter that it is not uncommon for multiple moons to eclipse the planet at the same time. Three of Jupiter's moons - Io, Ganymede, and Europa, create an eclipse every orbit. Saturn also has frequent eclipses. Seven of its moons are large enough to cast an umbra on the planet's clouds, and during certain times of its year some of the moons cause eclipses daily. Also, technically speaking, Saturn’s rings create a partial eclipse all the time, though the extent of the shadow varies depending on the season. Eclipses are actually extremely rare on Uranus. This is because the planet’s axis is tilted almost 90 degrees from the orbital plane (for comparison, Earth is only tilted 23.5 degrees). Since Uranus's moons orbit along the plane of its equator, this tilt means that their orbital paths only line up between Uranus and the Sun for a brief period about every 42 years. The first ever photo of an eclipse on Uranus was taken in 2006 by the Hubble Space Telescope as the Moon Arial passed in front of Uranus. The last time the moons could eclipse Uranus was in 1965, when telescope technology simply could not produce the resolution necessary to witness them, and when Voyager 2 flew by the planet in 1986 the orbital planes of the moons were not aligned to cause eclipses. Like Saturn, Neptune has seven moons that can eclipse the planet. Eclipses on Neptune are usually rare due to its relatively large axial tilt of 28 degrees and extremely long orbital period. Only during two brief periods of its 165 year orbit do the orbital planes of the moons line up with the Sun to produce umbras on Neptune’s clouds. However, during those periods eclipses are fairly common. Voyager 2 managed to capture the moon Despina eclipsing Neptune during its 1989 flyby. As for planets orbiting other stars, we simply don't know for sure. Astronomers have yet to confirm the existence of any moons orbiting exoplanets. That said, given the prevalence of eclipsing moons in our own solar system, there's really no reason to believe there aren't other planets in the universe with eclipses as glorious -if not moreso - than our own.

Lions and leopards tend to hunt the same prey so lions generally attack leopards on sight in order to reduce competition for resources. Leopons have been bred in captivity, however, and several taxidermied specimens have been preserved.

Question: Are clouds and steam just tiny water droplets? If so, should they have the same density as water, which is much heavier than air, and should sink to the ground fast? Why are they not sinking?
Answer: Clouds and steam are not drops of water, they are water vapor, which is water molecules in gaseous form. Water vapor is less dense than oxygen and nitrogen gasses, the two main components of the atmosphere, and thus rises upwards. Large amounts of atmospheric water vapor form clouds. When the vapor cools and condenses, it forms water droplets which are liquid and thus denser than the atmospheric gasses. These drops fall to the ground as rain.

Question: How are birds able to swallow very large fish that we would choke trying? I mean they don't unhinge their jaws like snakes.

Question: Why do people think being LGBTQ is natural?
Answer: Same-sex sexual behavior has been observed in over 1,500 animal species. There are entire species of lizards that are exclusively female, such as the New Mexico whiptail. They reproduce via parthenogenesis, or natural cloning, but the whole process only starts when two females engage in a mating ritual. In a survey of mating behavior among giraffes in Tanzania, 94% of matings occured between two or more males, with male/female matings occuring only 6% of the time. Male giraffes engaged in “necking,” a form of foreplay Bonobos engage in sexual encounters multiple times a day, with no discernable preference for the gender of their mate. Male/male, female/female, and female/male pairings all occur with approximately the same frequency. Aside from humans, bonobos are the only primates that have sex face-to-face and are the only other primates that engage in tongue-kissing. There are many, many species that transition from one biological sex to another. Clownfish are famous for having schools made up of a single dominant female and numerous males. When the female dies, the oldest male in the school becomes the dominant female. Many species of wrasse start life as females and transition to males. A species of starfish, the Nepanthia belcheri, start out male, become female as they grow, then upon reaching their largest size, split into two males, starting the cycle over again. As for the “Qs,” one of the most dramatic examples of a non-binary animal is the lion. Five known wild females and a few captive females have grown manes and taken on a mixture of male and female tasks within the pride. They tend to be larger than the females, but smaller than the males and possess narrower heads like the lionesses. Mmamoriri, one of the most famous examples, was born female, possesses XX chromosomes (ruling out Klinefelter's Syndrome, a condition where a female has XXY chromosomes), and engages in hunts like other lionesses, but has a thick black mane and engages in territorial defense like a male. Mmamoriri before growing a mane vs after: Mmamoriri (on the right) with a biological male So there you have it. Lesbian lizards, gay giraffes, bisexual bonobos, trans starfish, and queer lions, all examples of LGBTQ creatures in nature. Of course, there are many, many, many more examples in the animal kingdom. Heck, my family had a pair of gay frogs as pets more than a decade before Alex Jones started freaking out about them. Humans are simply another example. And since the definition of “natural” is “existing in or caused by nature; not made or caused by humankind,” and all these examples occur in nature without human interference, that means that being LGBTQ is by definition natural.

Question: If Fox news is according to the left, such a discredited news source, how do you explain how they beat CNN and MSNBC in ratings for so many years in a row?
Answer: Congratulations, your logical fallacy is argumentum ad populum! Argumentum ad populum, also known as “appeal to popularity,” is any argument that states that, just because many people like (or dislike, or believe) something, it must be good (or bad, or true). This is a common fallacy often found in advertising, insisting that a brand must be good because it is the most popular. This also pops up in politics, where people insist that a law or policy must be good because the majority of people support it. The flaw in the argument is that the majority of people can be wrong. For instance, during the Civil Rights movement in the 1960s, the majority of Americans still believed that Jim Crow laws were morally acceptable, despite history showing this not to be the case. With the specific examples of Fox News, the reason it has such a high viewership is that it is the only mainstream news outlet with a specifically conservative bias. When people want non-biased news reporting they have a lot of options: CNN, network news stations like NBC, CBS, ABC, etc, NPR, BBC, etc. This means that the number or people seeking out this type of news is going to be split up among multiple channels, while the conservative audience is going to be primarily concentrated on Fox News. The ratings have nothing to do with the journalistic integrity of the channel, however. It's merely a reflection of Fox News' market dominance of the conservative news audience.

Question: Jupiter has nearly 10,000 trojan asteroids. It hasn't cleared its orbit, so how can it be classed as a planet?
Answer: According to the International Astronomical Union - the organization that developed the current scientific definition of a planet in 2006 - a planet has cleared its orbit when it is gravitationally dominant in its region, with no other bodies of comparable size other than its natural satellites or otherwise under its gravitational influence. (Emphasis mine) No Jupiter Trojan asteroid (or any other non-stellar object in the solar system for that matter) comes close to matching Jupiter's size, and they are all captured in the Lagrange-4 and 5 points. These are areas of gravitational equilibrium between the Sun and Jupiter where small bodies can remain in a relatively static distance from Jupiter for millions of not billions of years. The L-4 point is about 60° ahead of Jupiter and the L-5 point about 60° behind, but the Jupiter Trojans are still gravitationally influenced by Jupiter and thus do not pose any problem for Jupiter's classification as a planet.

Question: Has the Earth ever had more than one moon in history?
Answer: Around 4.5 billion years ago, when the Solar System was brand new, Earth shared its orbit with another planet. This planet, Theia, was about the size of Mars. The thing is, planet-sized objects can only share an orbit in a stable manner if the larger planet is at least 25 times more massive than the smaller one. Earth was only around 4 times as massive as Theia, so Theia’s orbit destabilized and the smaller planet began falling towards Earth. Theia struck Earth and exploded, instantly liquefying Earth's surface and blasting massive amounts of debris into orbit. Over time, much of this debris fell back to Earth, and some more was thrown out of Earth's orbit to form asteroids, but a significant amount of the debris formed a stable orbit around Earth in the form of a ring system. Over time, the debris in the ring system began to gravitationally clump together, eventually forming the Moon. It's quite possible that some of these clumps formed small moons before eventually being pulled into the Moon itself.

Question: Why was the B-24 Liberator considered a better bomber than B-17?
Answer: It wasn't particularly popular among the air crews that operated it but it was more popular with the top brass. B-24 crews gave it the unflattering nicknames “the flying bathtub” or “the flying boxcar” due to its ungainly profile and poor flight handling, and air crews typically favored the B-17 over the B-24. It also had a lower flight ceiling and was less durable than the B-17. On the other hand, the Liberator had a larger bomb capacity and a longer operational range which made it suited to a wider variety of missions and environments than the Flying Fortress. For instance, the B-24's longer range made it much more suited for bombing missions in the Pacific Theater than the B-17, which was eventually phased out of the theater entirely by 1943. The B-24 was also the first Allied bomber capable of plugging the “Mid-Atlantic Gap,” the area of the Atlantic previously too distant from land for bombers to provide air cover. The B-24 was used to great effect in maritime and anti-submarine patrol roles. This extra versatility made the Liberator more popular among the Allied leadership and led the B-24 Liberator to become not only the most produced bomber, but the most produced multi-engine aircraft in history. Question: What are the reasons that both geology and paleontology are not considered by any means true history and instead are just considered a subcategory of science?
Answer: “History” in an academic sense is limited to the study of human activity after the invention of writing. Archaeology typically focuses on the study of humans before the invention of writing, though there is fairly significant overlap between history and archaeology as different cultures developed writing at different times, if they even developed writing at all. Paleontology focuses on non-human life prior to the start of the Holocene Era 11,500 years ago. Geology focuses on the study of rocks and minerals and how they change over time. Academically speaking, paleontology and geology are not included under the discipline of history because, even though they deal with the past, they do not focus on human activity.

Question: Why is it that ancient artifacts like fossils and civilizational remains are buried deep underground. It's not like there's more dirt, so is this stuff sinking?
Answer: This question contains a couple false premises. Firstly, there actually is more dirt. Dirt is decayed organic matter like leaves and decomposed animal bodies. New soil accumulates at a rate of about one inch every 500–1000 years. On top of that, environmental factors can increase the build-up dramatically: windstorms can blow large amounts of sand and dust around, volcanic eruptions can drop several feet of ash at a time, floods deposit several inches of silt at a time, etc. Plants can grow in and around old structures very easily, eventually burying them under new forest growth. There are plenty of ways for ancient artifacts and even ancient cities to get buried even without sinking. That said, some buildings do sink over time, especially if they are built in swampy areas. The city of Venice, for instance, is sinking at an average rate of about 1.5 mm a year. However sinking is far from the only way for archaeological remains to end up underground. It's also rare for archaeological remains to be buried “deep” underground. Most archaeological digs are only a few inches deep. Those that are more than a foot deep tend to be in places with a lot of rapid deposition such as floodplains. As for fossils, most of them are tens to hundreds of millions of years old. This is a very simplified hypothetical: if a fossil died ten million years ago in a region where soil build-up occured at a steady rate of one inch every 500 years, then that would be enough time for the soil to accumulate 20,000 inches, or 1,666.7 ft. In addition, fossils are old enough that other factors come into play, such as glacial deposits and tectonic plate movements, which explains how fossils can be found so deep.
